newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Richard defends state stake in defence.
newsitem.headline: France's Richard defends state stake in defence.

text.p: Defence Minister Alain Richard strongly defended on Friday continued state ownership of an important part of the shares of French defence firms.
"We think this government has the ability to maintain a stake with decision-making power in defence industries," Richard told Radio Luxembourg.
He said the reasons for such arrangements were "understandable to everyone" including "many foreign countries".

He was responding to recent comments from British Aerospace Plc managing director John Weston about the French state's 100 percent stake in Aerospatiale and 50 percent stake in Dassault Aviation, which are slated to merge.

Weston told a French parliamentary committee on Wednesday that the holdings would be an obstacle to European defence industry consolidation, needed for Europe to compete effectively with the United States.
He said a regrouping of BAe, Germany's Daimler Aerospace and Aerospatiale-Dassault into a single defence firm was "the strict minimum to create a European company".

Richard responded that the government headed by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin believed it was possible to reconcile an important public stake in French defence firms with international market demands.
"Airbus has shown this for 25 years," he said.
He said opposition to this idea stemmed from ideological or commercial motives.

Aerospatiale is the French partner in the four-nation Airbus Industrie airliner marketing consortium, while Dassault makes warplanes. BAe, Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas SA are also Airbus partners.
Asked about a possible decision on a re-capitalisation of French arms-maker GIAT Industries, Richard was non-committal but praised the firm's effort to improve its financial condition.
"Giat is improving its situation, it is trying hard," he said. "In my opinion it is assuming its responsibilities like a major firm."
Giat is burdened with a 10 billion franc net loss following dollar hedging cover which went against it on a $3.6 billion contract for Leclerc battle tanks to the United Arab Emirates in 1993.
